title: GIFT: Gradient Informed Filtering for Distillation Augmented Reasoning RL
authors: Shijie Li, Yilin Gao, Tieyuan Chen, Yun Luo, Weiyao Lin, Hang Yu
abstract: Training large language models for complex reasoning tasks relies on two complementary signals: sparse, outcome-grounded reinforcement learning (RL) for correctness, and dense, token-level distillation for guidance. However, complementarity in supervision does not guarantee compatibility in optimization; imitation-focused distillation can conflict with the outcome-driven RL objective, and existing hybrids lack a principled resolution. We propose \textbf{GIFT} (\textbf{G}radient-\textbf{I}nformed \textbf{F}il\textbf{T}ering for Distillation-Augmented Reasoning RL), a novel method that directly addresses the allocation problem of which teacher updates to apply. GIFT performs a token-level geometric analysis, decomposing the distillation gradient into a component \textbf{parallel} to the RL gradient, which measures first-order conflict and provides a \textbf{safety} filter, and a component \textbf{orthogonal} to it, which quantifies novel directional guidance and provides a measure of \textbf{value}. This decomposition yields a principled scoring rule to rank token-level guidance. We combine this with a progressive \textbf{coverage annealing} schedule that shrinks the budget of tokens receiving distillation, ensuring that the most conflicting updates are discarded first while the most complementary ones are retained at full strength. This facilitates a smooth transition from dense, geometrically-filtered guidance to a pure, outcome-grounded objective at convergence. Extensive experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks show that GIFT consistently outperforms strong baselines across multiple model scales, achieving relative gains of up to 9.5\% on difficult mathematical reasoning tasks. Code: https://github.com/lilifree/GIFT

infographic.key_insight: GIFT selectively applies token-level teacher guidance based on its geometric compatibility with the reinforcement learning gradient.
infographic.engineering_relevance: GIFT offers a principled way to combine dense distillation with outcome-based RL while reducing conflicting updates during reasoning training.
method: Decompose distillation gradients into components parallel and orthogonal to the RL gradient to assess conflict and novel guidance.
Rank token-level guidance using these geometric signals, filtering conflicting updates while retaining complementary guidance at full strength.
Progressively reduce distillation coverage, transitioning to pure outcome-grounded RL at convergence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent improvements over strong baselines across mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks and multiple model scales, with relative gains up to 9.5% on difficult math tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Token-level gradient analysis may add training overhead; the abstract does not quantify its computational cost.
infographic.paper_title: GIFT: Gradient Informed Filtering for Distillation Augmented Reasoning RL

title: RoleFlow: Self-Evolving Multi-Role Agentic Collaboration via Structural Adaptation
authors: Yi Ge, Pan Wang, Xuehao Cui, Zian Zeng, Xu Hu, Heng Huang
abstract: Large language model (LLM) based multi-agent systems often rely on predefined collaboration structures, limiting their adaptability to evolving task requirements. Although recent approaches enable dynamic orchestration, trajectory-level rewards they apply assign one outcome to each decision, ofen struggling to identify the contributions of individual structural changes. We propose RoleFlow, a self-evolving multi-role agentic system that refines collaboration structures through feedback-driven atomic edits and on-demand role synthesis. To make structural adaptation learnable, we introduce Single-Edit Counterfactual Policy Optimization (SECPO), which evaluates each edit against its no-edit counterpart at the same chain state and assigns targeted credit to edit-specific tokens. Across seven benchmarks spanning four domains, RoleFlow achieves the optimal average performance, surpassing the strongest competitor by 4.7 points. It leads on all three multi-hop QA benchmarks by 3.2-7.5 F1 points and also shows supremacy on mathematical reasoning, web interaction, and code generation. Further analyses demonstrate cross-benchmark transferability, training-data efficiency, and cross-executor generalization.

infographic.key_insight: RoleFlow improves multi-agent collaboration by learning targeted structural edits and synthesizing roles on demand instead of relying on fixed workflows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive agent workflows could help engineering assistants adjust collaboration to changing reasoning, coding, and web-interaction tasks.
method: Refine collaboration structures through feedback-driven atomic edits.
Synthesize new agent roles on demand.
Use SECPO to compare each edit with a no-edit counterpart at the same chain state and credit edit-specific tokens.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across seven benchmarks in four domains, the abstract reports a 4.7-point average lead over the strongest competitor and 3.2–7.5 F1-point leads on three multi-hop QA benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Counterfactual edit evaluation may add execution cost; the abstract does not quantify this overhead.
infographic.paper_title: RoleFlow: Self-Evolving Multi-Role Agentic Collaboration via Structural Adaptation

title: Discovery of Singularities in Partial Differential Equations Using Adaptive Numerical Discretizations
authors: Allen Yang, Lucas Amoudruz, Petros Koumoutsakos
abstract: We compute self-similar singularity profiles of partial differential equations (PDEs) using adaptive numerical discretizations based on optimizing a discrete loss (ODIL). The fields are represented in overlapping local Chebyshev patches joined with a mapped asymptotic patch. After factoring out the leading power laws of solution ansatzes, their limiting amplitudes at infinity are determined by the optimization, eliminating domain truncation and prescribed far-field conditions. Adaptive refinement is guided by Chebyshev-coefficient decay, and the nonlinear least-squares problem is solved using automatically differentiated Gauss--Newton iterations with Levenberg--Marquardt damping. The method achieves O(10^{-14})-level accuracy for Burgers profiles, residuals of O(10^{-14}) to O(10^{-10}) for the generalized De Gregorio family, and of O(10^{-8}) in a local region for the two-dimensional Boussinesq equations. These results demonstrate that ODIL can identify singularity profiles for PDEs with high accuracy using adaptive numerical methods, complementing ongoing efforts that rely on artificial intelligence.

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive optimization of discrete PDE equations can recover highly accurate self-similar singularity profiles without prescribing far-field amplitudes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a high-accuracy numerical tool for studying PDE blow-up while avoiding finite-domain truncation and prescribed far-field conditions.
method: Represent fields with overlapping local Chebyshev patches and a mapped asymptotic patch.
Factor out leading power laws, optimize limiting amplitudes, and refine using Chebyshev-coefficient decay.
Solve the discrete nonlinear least-squares problem with automatic differentiation, Gauss–Newton iterations, and Levenberg–Marquardt damping.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports O(10^-14)-level accuracy for Burgers profiles, O(10^-14)–O(10^-10) residuals for generalized De Gregorio equations, and O(10^-8) residuals in a local region for 2D Boussinesq equations.
infographic.watch_item: Small numerical residuals do not establish rigorous singularity existence, and the reported Boussinesq accuracy is local.
infographic.paper_title: Discovery of Singularities in Partial Differential Equations Using Adaptive Numerical Discretizations

title: A Transformer-based Approach for Real-time Multi-agent Path Planning with Varying Initial/Final Conditions
authors: Qian Zhang, Shanqing Liu, Jerome Darbon, George Karniadakis
abstract: We address the problem of real-time multi-agent path planning under prescribed initial and final configurations, formulated as a high-dimensional optimal control problem subject to inter-agent collision avoidance and obstacle constraints. Classical solvers based on the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation or Pontryagin's maximum principle (PMP) become computationally intractable as the number of agents grows, due to the curse of dimensionality and the non-convexity introduced by interaction constraints. We propose OCFormer, a transformer-based neural network that parameterizes the inverse of a coordinate transformation mapping a simple, analytically tractable latent space, in which agents evolve independently under a decoupled Hamiltonian, to the physical space of the coupled, interacting system. The model is trained by minimizing a physics-informed loss comprising the Hamiltonian ODE residual from the PMP and a boundary matching term, without requiring pre-computed trajectory data. The self-attention mechanism endows OCFormer with permutation equivariance over agents, a structural symmetry that prior symplectic network approaches do not natively enforce. When trained on a distribution of boundary conditions, the amortized OCFormer produces near-optimal trajectories for unseen initial and final configurations in a single forward pass ($\sim$220ms), enabling real-time inference without retraining. We further introduce a lightweight transfer learning framework that adapts a pretrained OCFormer to out-of-distribution perturbations in seconds via L-BFGS fine-tuning. Numerical experiments on two- and three-dimensional multi-agent navigation with up to 128 agents demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of the proposed approach.

infographic.key_insight: OCFormer learns a transformer-based mapping from simple, independent latent dynamics to coupled multi-agent trajectories, enabling near-optimal planning for unseen start and goal configurations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Amortized inference could support responsive robot-fleet navigation under collision and obstacle constraints without solving a new optimal control problem from scratch.
method: Map analytically tractable latent dynamics to interacting agents in physical space.
Train without precomputed trajectories using PMP Hamiltonian ODE residuals and boundary matching.
Use permutation-equivariant self-attention and L-BFGS fine-tuning for out-of-distribution conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 2D and 3D navigation experiments with up to 128 agents, approximately 220 ms forward-pass inference, and adaptation to out-of-distribution perturbations in seconds.
infographic.watch_item: Physics-informed training does not by itself establish hard collision-avoidance guarantees; safety and timing need validation on target hardware and deployment scenarios.
infographic.paper_title: A Transformer-based Approach for Real-time Multi-agent Path Planning with Varying Initial/Final Conditions

title: Reinforcement Learning for Global-Local Control of Dynamic Networks with Applications to Systemic Risk
authors: Nils Detering, Florian Grell, Thilo Meyer-Brandis
abstract: We propose a reinforcement learning framework for solving control problems on dynamic networks, where control decisions consist of a combination of graph-level (global) and node-level (local) actions. To exploit the underlying network structure in a policy-gradient algorithm, we introduce a message-passing neural network architecture with separate global and local policy heads. The architecture ensures that the resulting policies satisfy natural permutation symmetries and transparency constraints. Our main theoretical contribution is an analysis of the robustness and regularity properties of the proposed architecture. We derive explicit Lipschitz bounds with respect to both parameter and input perturbations and use these estimates to establish convergence guarantees for a projected policy-gradient algorithm. The resulting constants reveal how architectural choices and graph characteristics influence sensitivity to input perturbations and the convergence behavior of gradient-based optimization methods. As an application, we study the management of systemic risk in financial networks, where a regulator allocates capital interventions across interconnected institutions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed reinforcement learning architecture outperforms standard architectures based on feedforward neural networks while the learned policies fulfill desirable symmetry and transparency constraints. The algorithm scales to large networks and effectively combines global budget decisions with local allocation policies by exploiting the underlying graph structure.

infographic.key_insight: A message-passing reinforcement learning architecture coordinates global and node-level network control while preserving permutation symmetries and transparency constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports scalable control of interconnected systems, including joint decisions about intervention budgets and institution-level capital allocations in financial networks.
method: Use message passing with separate global and local policy heads.
Derive explicit Lipschitz bounds for parameter and input perturbations.
Use these bounds to establish projected policy-gradient convergence guarantees.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments on systemic-risk management report better performance than feedforward-network baselines and scalability to large networks, though the abstract provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Sensitivity and optimization behavior depend on architectural choices and graph characteristics, so robustness should be checked for each deployment setting.
infographic.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning for Global-Local Control of Dynamic Networks with Applications to Systemic Risk

title: ORSMT: Unleashing the Potential of Satisfiability Modulo Theories for Semantic Verification and Repair in LLM-Based Optimization
authors: Rui Zhang, Chenyu Zhou, Jianghao Lin, Yaoxin Wu, Dongdong Ge, Wen Song
abstract: Large language models increasingly automate optimization modeling from natural language problems, producing written mathematics, solver code and a returned report. Verifying one optimization problem across these artifacts requires semantic comparison: unequal models can attain the same objective, equivalent models can use different auxiliary variables, and mutually consistent artifacts can omit the same source requirement. ORSMT provides a typed semantic interface and exact SMT relation queries. It aligns observable decisions, projects auxiliary variables, proves or refutes feasible region and objective relations, localizes refutations to implicated rows or domains and links source texts when available. It then reconstructs one artifact from another, and each adopted candidate passes the required relation checks. Across 3,034 problems and six generator sizes, ORSMT improves the model-code match rate in all 72 benchmark and generator combinations before selection. Protected selection raises the aggregate rate from 43.2% to 88.2% and the share that are both correct and matched from 25.2% to 40.2%. On the 1,905 refuted outputs, certified voting under the shared fallback makes 50.9% of outputs correct and matched, compared with 44.8% for ReLoop and 49.4% for Opt-Verifier. A separate one-round source revision followed by exact reconstruction restores a model-code match for 84.4% of the refuted pairs.

infographic.key_insight: ORSMT uses exact SMT checks to detect and repair semantic mismatches between optimization models and solver code, beyond agreement on objective values.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It helps engineers validate LLM-generated optimization pipelines by checking feasible regions and objectives while accounting for auxiliary variables.
method: Align observable decisions through a typed semantic interface and project away auxiliary variables.
Prove or refute feasible-region and objective relations, localizing failures to rows or domains.
Reconstruct artifacts and adopt repair candidates only after required relation checks pass.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 3,034 problems and six generator sizes, protected selection increased aggregate model-code matching from 43.2% to 88.2%, while correct-and-matched outputs rose from 25.2% to 40.2%.
infographic.watch_item: Model-code agreement does not guarantee source correctness: both artifacts can omit the same requirement, making source-level validation essential.
infographic.paper_title: ORSMT: Unleashing the Potential of Satisfiability Modulo Theories for Semantic Verification and Repair in LLM-Based Optimization

title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping
authors: Chengxi Li, Hanlin Wu, Zhicheng Cai, Huan-ang Gao, Wei-Ying Ma, Jingjing Liu
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) based on PPO-style clipping has become an effective approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, standard token-level clipping measures policy change only through the conditional probability of the current token, while the prefix conditioning context is itself generated by the policy. This mismatch becomes especially consequential in long-response and off-policy training. We reformulate autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and derive its performance-difference identity under behavior-policy sampling. The resulting change of measure identifies the cumulative likelihood ratio of the generated prefix as the exact importance weight for each stepwise policy-improvement term. Starting from the monotonic-improvement principle of trust-region policy optimization, we then construct a prefix-level trust region using the exact reverse-KL coordinate $r-1-\log r$, whose behavior-policy expectation equals the corresponding prefix-distribution KL divergence. This yields EPIC, a PPO-style sequence-clipping method that directly regulates prefix-level policy drift without relying on a local quadratic approximation or expert-routing replay. Experiments on off-policy reinforcement learning with a sparse mixture-of-experts language model show that EPIC consistently outperforms standard and sequence-level clipping baselines across mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, while remaining competitive with routing-replay-based alternatives. Code is available at https://github.com/LiChengxi666/EPIC.

infographic.key_insight: EPIC constrains policy drift over generated prefixes, addressing changes in context that token-level PPO clipping does not directly control.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Prefix-level clipping offers a way to stabilize off-policy LLM reinforcement learning without expert-routing replay, particularly for long responses.
method: Model autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process.
Derive cumulative prefix likelihood ratios as exact importance weights for stepwise policy improvement.
Use the exact reverse-KL coordinate r−1−log(r) to construct a prefix-level trust region and PPO-style clipping.
infographic.evidence_signal: In off-policy training of a sparse mixture-of-experts language model, EPIC consistently outperformed standard and sequence-level clipping baselines on mathematical-reasoning benchmarks and remained competitive with routing-replay alternatives.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative gains or model-scale details, so generalization beyond the tested sparse mixture-of-experts setting remains unclear.
infographic.paper_title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping

title: Minimax Rates for imperfect Physics-Informed Regression
authors: Nathan Doumèche
abstract: Physics-informed machine learning incorporates physical knowledge into data-driven models, often through a partial differential equation (PDE) that the target is assumed to satisfy. However, how much this knowledge improves statistical performance remains unclear, especially when the physical model is imperfect. Since satisfying a PDE implies being differentiable, a natural benchmark for physics-informed regression is the best achievable performance when smoothness is the only prior information about the target function. We show that there is a characteristic threshold for the modeling error above which the physical prior cannot improve the convergence rate. The form of this threshold is common to every linear PDE and certain nonlinear PDEs. Below it, the gain depends on the equation type. For classes of elliptic and hyperbolic PDEs with constant coefficients, we establish convergence rates that improve continuously as the modeling error decreases, and prove their minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors. With exact physics, the rates correspond to learning in dimension d-1 rather than d, reflecting the freedom left by unknown boundary or initial data. We also give conditions for computing the estimator with near-linear complexity and show how to tune its hyperparameters without knowing the modeling error.

infographic.key_insight: Imperfect PDE knowledge improves regression convergence rates only below a modeling-error threshold; with exact physics, studied PDE classes yield rates corresponding to dimension d−1 rather than d.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results clarify when physical constraints can improve data efficiency and provide conditions for near-linear estimator computation and tuning without knowing the modeling error.
method: Benchmark physics-informed regression against regression using only smoothness assumptions.
Derive modeling-error thresholds for all linear PDEs and certain nonlinear PDEs.
Establish minimax-optimal rates up to logarithmic factors for classes of constant-coefficient elliptic and hyperbolic PDEs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence rates and minimax guarantees, but describes no empirical datasets or experiments.
infographic.watch_item: The detailed rate guarantees cover specific PDE classes, and near-linear computation requires additional conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Minimax Rates for imperfect Physics-Informed Regression

title: Edit, Don't Imitate: Minimal-Edit On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning
authors: Wen Ye, Ailin Deng, Zirui Wang, Shixing Yu, Han Zhang, Tian Yun
abstract: Visual mathematical reasoning can fail before reasoning begins: when a vision-language model (VLM) misreads a diagram, subsequent reasoning proceeds from false premises. This perceptual bottleneck is especially pronounced in smaller models, while accurate textual descriptions can substantially narrow the gap to larger models. Because obtaining such descriptions at inference requires additional annotation or model calls, we propose minimal-edit corrective on-policy distillation. Using reference figure descriptions and verified reference solutions as training-only information, a teacher scores incorrect student rollouts under a minimal-edit objective, and only teacher-disfavored tokens contribute to the corrective loss. Correct rollouts receive task-reward reinforcement learning. This preserves on-policy supervision while avoiding full-response imitation. Across model scales, the method requires no descriptions at test time and meets or exceeds the corresponding base model supplied with a reference figure description at inference. It also improves perception-oriented performance, particularly low-level geometric perception, and transfers to external mathematics and perception benchmarks. Because the minimal-edit teacher evaluates corrections rather than generating its own solution, the method remains effective with a frozen same-size teacher, although its gains are smaller than with a larger teacher on most metrics.

infographic.key_insight: Correcting only teacher-disfavored tokens in incorrect student rollouts improves visual mathematical reasoning without requiring figure descriptions at inference.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Training-time perceptual correction can strengthen smaller vision-language models without adding annotation or teacher calls at deployment.
method: Generate on-policy student rollouts for visual math problems.
Use training-only reference descriptions and verified solutions to score incorrect rollouts under a minimal-edit objective, applying corrective loss only to teacher-disfavored tokens.
Apply task-reward reinforcement learning to correct rollouts rather than imitating full teacher responses.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across model scales, the method meets or exceeds corresponding base models given reference descriptions at inference, improves low-level geometric perception, and transfers to external math and perception benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Training requires reference figure descriptions and verified solutions; a frozen same-size teacher remains effective but yields smaller gains than a larger teacher on most metrics.
infographic.paper_title: Edit, Don't Imitate: Minimal-Edit On-Policy Distillation for Multimodal Reasoning

title: Breaking the high-degree barrier in Lehmer's problem with a human-AI discovery loop
authors: Yuri Chervonyi, Sergei Gukov, Thang Luong
abstract: While artificial intelligence has made rapid progress in mathematical reasoning, many open problems depend on structure that is revealed only through large-scale computational exploration and analytical synthesis. One such example is Lehmer's problem from 1933. It asks whether the Mahler measure of an integer polynomial, which measures how far its roots stray from the unit circle, can be made arbitrarily small. Previously, constructing irreducible polynomials with integer coefficients and small Mahler measure has been carried out systematically only for even degrees $d \le 180$. At higher degrees, Boyd's analytical one-parameter family frequently factors, skipping nearly 50% of target degrees and leaving no general construction for arbitrary $d$. Here, we address the high-degree regime through a human-AI discovery loop, in which we extend the conversational prompting with a fast numerical pipeline, an exact symbolic verifier, and large-scale distributed search. The AI agent prototypes numerical and symbolic solvers locally, launches parallel searches across distributed clusters and works with the human researcher to extract and verify mathematical hypotheses. Through this interactive loop, we derive a five-parameter construction, which we call the Generalized Boyd algorithm. It eliminates degree-skipping and constructs irreducible polynomials with Mahler measure strictly below Boyd's limit point $α_1 \approx 1.255434$ for every target degree. Evaluated across all even degrees up to 2000, our approach improves upon six previously published values and holds 99.6% of all best known records. With this work we release the verified dataset of polynomials with minimal Mahler measure across all studied even degrees.

infographic.key_insight: A human–AI discovery loop produced the five-parameter Generalized Boyd algorithm, eliminating degree-skipping when constructing irreducible integer polynomials with small Mahler measure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work demonstrates how fast numerical exploration, distributed computing, and exact symbolic verification can support reliable AI-assisted mathematical discovery.
method: Use an AI agent to prototype numerical and symbolic solvers.
Run parallel searches across distributed clusters.
Collaboratively extract hypotheses and verify candidate polynomials exactly.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across all even degrees up to 2000, the approach improves six previously published values and holds 99.6% of best-known records; the authors release a verified polynomial dataset.
infographic.watch_item: The reported evaluation covers even degrees up to 2000; these computational records do not resolve Lehmer’s problem.
infographic.paper_title: Breaking the high-degree barrier in Lehmer's problem with a human-AI discovery loop

title: Convergence of stochastic gradient descent for learning linear neural networks
authors: Gabin Maxime Nguegnang, Bubacarr Bah, Holger Rauhut, Ulrich Terstiege
abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is the cornerstone of modern deep learning, yet its theoretical convergence properties remain poorly understood in non-convex settings. To address this gap, we study SGD dynamics in deep linear neural networks - simplified models that retain key non-convex characteristics while remaining analytically tractable. Building on recent results for gradient descent, we extend convergence guarantees to SGD under regularized squared loss. We establish almost sure boundedness of SGD iterates. Using the framework of asymptotic pseudotrajectories from stochastic approximation theory, our analysis establishes then, for both deterministic and adaptive step-size choices, convergence of SGD to the set of critical points under mild conditions (without relying on Lipschitz properties or whitened data). To our knowledge, this is the first work providing almost sure convergence guarantees for SGD in deep linear networks, bridging the gap between theoretical optimization and practical stochastic training.

infographic.key_insight: The paper establishes almost sure boundedness and convergence of SGD to the set of critical points in deep linear networks trained with regularized squared loss.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results strengthen the theoretical foundations of stochastic training in a tractable non-convex model, but do not establish guarantees for nonlinear networks.
method: Extend gradient-descent convergence analysis to stochastic updates.
Establish almost sure boundedness of SGD iterates.
Use asymptotic pseudotrajectories to prove convergence under deterministic and adaptive step-size choices.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical guarantees under mild conditions, without relying on Lipschitz properties or whitened data; it describes no empirical evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Convergence to the critical-point set does not by itself guarantee convergence to a global optimum or provide a practical convergence rate.
infographic.paper_title: Convergence of stochastic gradient descent for learning linear neural networks

title: What the submission does not show: Complexifying cognitive offloading in students' mathematical work with LLMs
authors: Igor' Kontorovich, Miriam N. Wallach
abstract: A common concern is that using large language models (LLMs) lets students offload mathematical work that tasks are designed to elicit. Yet such claims often rest on outcomes (e.g., submitted solutions), rather than on evidence of students' work with LLMs. We followed 23 first-year linear algebra students as they solved three differently designed homework tasks with LLMs. Drawing on self-regulated learning and choice-affluent environments, we interpreted each of 429 prompts as a trace of a regulatory event and compared 59 chatlogs with the problem solutions the students submitted. Prompts formed five structures, casting the LLM mainly as a solver, explainer, or validator. The mix of structures shifted across the tasks, and ten of the 15 students who completed all three tasks changed their dominant structure. Most final submissions stayed close to LLM output, including those that followed exchanges in which students had explained, conjectured, and checked their own ideas. We conclude that an LLM-aided submission is not a trustworthy marker of students' offloading of the mathematical work, and that offloading needs to be examined in each regulatory space and part by part rather than as a whole.

infographic.key_insight: A submitted solution that closely matches LLM output does not reliably reveal how much mathematical thinking a student offloaded.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Educational AI tools should support process-level analysis of student–LLM interactions rather than infer cognitive engagement from final-answer similarity alone.
method: Followed first-year linear algebra students across three differently designed homework tasks.
Interpreted prompts as regulatory events using self-regulated learning and choice-affluent environments.
Compared chatlogs with submitted solutions and identified five interaction structures.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study analyzed 429 prompts across 59 chatlogs from 23 students; 10 of the 15 who completed all three tasks changed their dominant interaction structure.
infographic.watch_item: The small, course-specific sample limits generalization, and prompt traces do not directly measure all student thinking.
infographic.paper_title: What the submission does not show: Complexifying cognitive offloading in students' mathematical work with LLMs

title: Adaptive Grid Refinement for Optimal Feedback Control
authors: Alen E. Golpashin, Matthew T. Clark, Bruce A. Conway
abstract: This paper introduces an algorithmic approach for adaptive grid refinement for solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) partial differential equation (PDE) to obtain the optimal feedback control. Traditional grid generation methods often face challenges associated with state-space dimensionality, solution regularity, and large variations in the solution. Whereas fixed grid generation methods may fail to capture the intricate details of the optimal solution, our methodology addresses this challenge by dynamically refining the grid used to solve the HJB equation, thereby optimizing computational resource usage while targeting improved solution accuracy. The reinforcement learning (RL)-based approach presented in this study seeks to reduce the node population while constructing a grid with higher node density in regions with large discretization error.

infographic.key_insight: Reinforcement learning guides adaptive grid refinement for the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation, concentrating nodes where discretization error is large to support optimal feedback control.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Error-focused refinement could make feedback-control computation more resource-efficient than using a uniformly fine state-space grid.
method: Solve the HJB equation on a state-space grid.
Use an RL-based approach to adapt grid-node placement.
Target fewer total nodes while increasing density in high-error regions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes the approach and its intended efficiency and accuracy benefits but reports no benchmarks, quantitative results, or evaluation details.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability and accuracy gains remain unverified in the abstract, especially for high-dimensional state spaces.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive Grid Refinement for Optimal Feedback Control

title: Group Distributionally Robust Optimization over Decentralized Networks
authors: Haomin Bai, Junyan Sun, Quan Cheng, Yuanyu Wan, Lijun Zhang
abstract: We study group distributionally robust optimization (GDRO) over decentralized networks, where workers collaborate to learn robust models by minimizing the maximum local risk. Existing methods optimize only dual-regularized surrogates and establish guarantees for a globally averaged model that is not available to workers. In this paper, we directly optimize the original GDRO objective and establish guarantees for local models in semi-decentralized (SemiDec) and fully decentralized (Dec) settings. A key difficulty is that applying the primal-dual decomposition from centralized GDRO yields worker-dependent losses whose evaluation requires unavailable cross-worker information. To address this challenge, we develop a novel error decomposition that recasts decentralized GDRO as (i) a decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) problem and a prediction-with-expert-advice problem in SemiDec, and as (ii) two coupled D-OCO problems in Dec, with discrepancy terms capturing inconsistencies among local decisions. By isolating consensus errors in analysis, we develop modular frameworks that support different consensus routines. We then establish the \emph{first} per-worker convergence guarantees for optimizing the original GDRO objective over decentralized networks. Instantiations with accelerated gossip and Choco-gossip achieve an $O(\sqrt{(\log m)/T})$ convergence rate over $T$ update rounds, while experiments demonstrate improved worst-worker performance over baselines.

infographic.key_insight: The paper establishes the first per-worker convergence guarantees for directly optimizing the original group distributionally robust objective over decentralized networks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Workers can collaboratively learn models that minimize worst-worker risk without relying on a globally averaged model unavailable locally.
method: Decompose semi-decentralized GDRO into decentralized online convex optimization and prediction with expert advice.
Decompose fully decentralized GDRO into two coupled decentralized online convex optimization problems.
Isolate consensus errors to support modular consensus routines, including accelerated gossip and Choco-gossip.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an O(√(log m/T)) convergence rate over T update rounds and improved worst-worker performance over experimental baselines, without naming datasets or effect sizes.
infographic.watch_item: Practical communication costs and sensitivity to network connectivity are not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Group Distributionally Robust Optimization over Decentralized Networks

title: A Model-Free Continuous-Time RL Algorithm from Discrete-Time Off-Policy Data with End-to-End Guarantees
authors: Chaorui Yao, Yuming Paul Zhang, Lin Yang, Yuhua Zhu
abstract: In this paper, we study continuous-time reinforcement learning, where the state follows an unknown stochastic differential equation but only a fixed off-policy batch of discrete-time transitions is available. Standard discrete-time Q-learning becomes problematic as the sampling interval shrinks, because differences between action values vanish. Continuous-time alternatives, such as Deep Advantage Updating and martingale q-learning, preserve the action signal but jointly learn a value function and an action-dependent critic. Building on the PhiBE-Q formulation (arXiv:2606.21925), we develop a model-free PhiBE policy iteration (PhiBE-PI) framework that uses a single state-action critic while preserving the continuous-time action-ranking scale. At each iteration, the framework learns the critic directly from sampled increments and uses it to improve the policy. The same batch is reused throughout, without explicitly estimating the drift or diffusion. We further develop an implementation under linear function approximation and establish a local end-to-end suboptimality guarantee for the learned policy. Our analysis quantifies how errors from time discretization, function approximation, and finite-sample policy evaluation propagate through policy iteration. It accounts for the dependence of successive policies on the reused data, so the guarantee does not require a fresh batch at each iteration. Moreover, we identify a bias-variance trade-off: smaller sampling intervals improve the approximation to the continuous-time problem but can increase statistical error at a fixed sample size. Thus, finer time discretization does not necessarily lead to better policy performance.

infographic.key_insight: PhiBE-PI learns continuous-time policies from a fixed batch of discrete-time, off-policy transitions using one state-action critic while preserving the action-ranking signal.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports continuous-time control learning from logged transitions without explicitly estimating system drift or diffusion.
method: Fit a single state-action critic directly from sampled increments.
Improve the policy and reuse the same batch across iterations.
Use linear function approximation with a local end-to-end suboptimality guarantee.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical error bounds covering time discretization, function approximation, finite samples, and adaptive data reuse, but gives no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Smaller sampling intervals reduce discretization error but can increase statistical error at fixed sample size, so finer sampling need not improve policy performance.
infographic.paper_title: A Model-Free Continuous-Time RL Algorithm from Discrete-Time Off-Policy Data with End-to-End Guarantees

title: The generic splitting type of the logarithmic bundle of an arrangement of at most sixteen lines is combinatorial
authors: Cristian Anghel, Rares Stan
abstract: Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an arrangement of $d$ lines in $\mathbb{P}^2_\mathbb{C}$ and let $\mathcal{T}\langle\mathcal{A}\rangle$ be its bundle of logarithmic vector fields. On a general line, $\mathcal{T}\langle\mathcal{A}\rangle$ splits as $\mathcal{O}(-k)\oplus\mathcal{O}(k+1-d)$ with $k=\min\{\mathrm{mdr}(\mathcal{A}),\lfloor\frac{d-1}{2}\rfloor\}$, where $\mathrm{mdr}$ is the minimal degree of a Jacobian syzygy. We prove that $k$ is determined by the intersection lattice whenever $d\le16$, answering in this range a question of Cook, Harbourne, Migliore and Nagel. Since freeness can be read off from $k$ and $c_2(\mathcal{T}\langle\mathcal{A}\rangle)$, this strengthens Terao's freeness conjecture in this range; in particular we obtain a proof of Terao's conjecture for $14$ lines that uses it only for $13$ lines. For any number $d$ of lines, it follows that $\mathrm{mdr}$ is determined by the lattice whenever $\mathrm{mdr}\le6$ and $2\mathrm{mdr}\le d-3$, and that Terao's conjecture holds for every free arrangement whose smaller exponent is at most $7$. The proof reduces the question to critical arrangements: $2s+3$ lines, each containing at most $s+1$ intersection points, with $\mathrm{mdr}=s$. For these, the inflection polynomial of the minimal derivation factors as $Q_\mathcal{A} R$ with $R\in H^0(\mathcal{I}_Z^2(s-3))$, where $Z$ is the zero scheme of the derivation, of length $ν=c_2(\mathcal{T}\langle\mathcal{A}\rangle)-s(s+2)$. For $s\le5$ this forces $ν\le1$, and Chern class arguments then reduce everything to Terao's conjecture for $13$ lines. For $s=6$ we show $ν\le3$, using a Riccati equation along multiple components of $R$, Ziegler's multirestriction, and local computations verified by computer algebra; an exhaustive enumeration of the 26,265,318 candidate lattices with $ν\in\{2,3\}$ that satisfy Bojanowski's inequality completes the proof.

infographic.key_insight: For arrangements of at most 16 complex projective lines, the intersection lattice determines the generic splitting type of the logarithmic bundle.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For computational algebra tools, the theorem allows this geometric invariant to be inferred from intersection combinatorics within the proven range.
method: Reduce to critical arrangements with 2s+3 lines and minimal Jacobian syzygy degree s.
Bound the derivation’s zero scheme using inflection-polynomial factorization and Chern classes.
Combine Riccati equations, Ziegler multirestriction, computer algebra, and exhaustive lattice enumeration.
infographic.evidence_signal: The proof includes computer-algebra-verified local computations and exhaustive enumeration of 26,265,318 candidate lattices satisfying Bojanowski’s inequality.
infographic.watch_item: The general splitting-type result is limited to at most 16 lines; extensions to arbitrary line counts require additional syzygy-degree or freeness conditions.
infographic.paper_title: The generic splitting type of the logarithmic bundle of an arrangement of at most sixteen lines is combinatorial

title: OptScientist: Automated Discovery of Optimization Laws
authors: Ma ZhenYao, Yue Liang, Jian-Qiao Zhu
abstract: Many scientific phenomena are best understood as outcomes of underlying optimization problems, yet automated scientific discovery has largely focused on recovering equations that describe observed input-output patterns. We introduce OptScientist, a novel automated framework for discovering compact symbolic optimization laws directly from data. OptScientist comprises (i) a model that infers symbolic optimization problems by first learning to represent data as an optimization problem and then extracting its symbolic form, and (ii) an LLM agentic system embedding the model in a discovery process that integrates theoretical priors from scientific literature, discovers candidate laws, abstracts their underlying mechanisms, and suggests new data to collect. We first evaluate OptScientist on OptFeynman, a novel benchmark of 99 physics-derived optimization problems, where OptScientist recovers ground-truth laws for over 80% of the problems and remains robust to noisy contextual information, while substantially outperforming machine-learning, symbolic, and LLM-based model-discovery baselines. On human risky choice and central-bank monetary policy, OptScientist discovers compact symbolic optimization laws that achieve held-out predictive performance competitive with leading baselines, while using few parameters and substantially fewer tokens than LLM baselines. Overall, OptScientist extends automated scientific discovery to uncovering optimization laws that generate observed phenomena, enabling automated theory building across the physical, biological, behavioral, and social sciences.

infographic.key_insight: OptScientist discovers compact symbolic optimization laws that explain observations as outcomes of underlying optimization problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could help engineers infer interpretable objectives and constraints from observed system behavior.
method: Learn to represent observed data as an optimization problem, then extract its symbolic form.
Use an LLM agent to integrate scientific priors and discover candidate laws.
Abstract candidate mechanisms and suggest new data to collect.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the 99-problem OptFeynman benchmark, OptScientist recovers over 80% of ground-truth laws; on risky choice and monetary policy, it achieves competitive held-out prediction with few parameters.
infographic.watch_item: Predictive accuracy alone does not establish that a discovered objective or constraint is the true mechanism generating the data.
infographic.paper_title: OptScientist: Automated Discovery of Optimization Laws

title: Curvature-Scaled Sharpness-Aware Minimization: Convergence Beyond Smoothness
authors: Dimitris Oikonomou, Nicolas Loizou
abstract: Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) has established itself as a widely used method for training deep neural networks. Despite its popularity, existing convergence guarantees for SAM-type methods require smoothness, a restrictive assumption. Generalized smoothness conditions have recently been proposed in the analysis of gradient methods but remain underexplored for SAM. To analyze the effect of SAM's perturbation under generalized smoothness, we use relative gradient distortion to quantify how the sharpness-aware direction departs from the original gradient. Under $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness, we show that this distortion can become unbounded near stationarity for SAM and at large gradients for its unnormalized variant (USAM), with examples where SAM cycles and USAM diverges. We then establish a necessary condition for uniform distortion control among perturbations along the gradient whose nonnegative multipliers depend only on its norm. Motivated by this condition, we propose Curvature-Scaled SAM (CS-SAM), which scales both the perturbation and the descent step by suitable curvature upper bounds, and prove that it uniformly bounds the distortion. Under both $(L_0,L_1)$- and $(H_0,H_1)$-smoothness, we establish deterministic $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ rates for the best squared gradient norm on nonconvex objectives, last-iterate $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ rates for the function gap on convex objectives with a minimizer, and linear convergence under the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. With zero perturbation, our guarantees recover the rates for gradient descent with $(L_0,L_1)$- or $(H_0,H_1)$-based step-sizes. Minibatch experiments on computer vision tasks demonstrate competitive performance for both variants, with the $(H_0,H_1)$ variant achieving the highest mean best-test accuracy in all four settings against tuned SAM and USAM with constant and cosine annealing schedules.

infographic.key_insight: Curvature-Scaled SAM controls gradient distortion under generalized smoothness, enabling convergence guarantees where standard SAM can cycle and unnormalized SAM can diverge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Curvature-aware perturbations and descent steps offer a principled alternative to SAM for neural-network training beyond standard smoothness assumptions.
method: Measure relative gradient distortion caused by sharpness-aware perturbations.
Scale both perturbation and descent step using curvature upper bounds.
Prove deterministic O(1/T) rates for nonconvex stationarity and convex function gaps, plus linear convergence under the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition.
infographic.evidence_signal: In minibatch computer-vision experiments, the (H0,H1) variant achieved the highest mean best-test accuracy in all four settings against tuned SAM and USAM with constant and cosine-annealing schedules.
infographic.watch_item: The stated convergence guarantees are deterministic; practical minibatch use also depends on choosing suitable curvature upper bounds.
infographic.paper_title: Curvature-Scaled Sharpness-Aware Minimization: Convergence Beyond Smoothness

title: Local Work, Global Progress: A Convergence Theory of AI Agent Collaboration
authors: Ivan Ilin, Peter Richtárik
abstract: Teams of large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly applied to complex tasks, but their collaboration protocols are mostly designed empirically, without convergence guarantees. We formalize collaborative problem solving as block optimization: each agent improves one part of a shared solution, guided by its local objective plus a correction for how its changes affect the other parts. A coordinator checks every proposal against the global objective and merges proposals that do not interfere with each other. We prove linear convergence up to an error floor that vanishes when the corrections are exact. Interfering proposals can also be merged once their combination has been checked; the rate then depends on how well the proposals actually combine, not on worst-case interactions. With GPT-OSS-120B agents on robot routing, a three-agent team finds collision-free plans in every run, better than those of a single agent that controls all robots. On a larger routing task, a six-agent team completes its search about twice as fast as the single agent (in median). Merging the best checked combination of proposals, rather than only proposals that do not interfere, cuts the team's search time by about 30%. With constants measured on the runs, our convergence bound holds in every round and follows the observed progress. We also test the theory on query planning in SQLite and on a synthetic task.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-agent collaboration can be modeled as block optimization with provable linear convergence to an error floor that vanishes when cross-agent corrections are exact.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A coordinator that checks proposals against a global objective can turn parallel agent work into reliable progress while safely merging compatible updates.
method: Each agent improves one solution block using a local objective plus a correction for effects on other blocks.
A coordinator checks global improvement and merges noninterfering proposals or explicitly checked combinations.
The convergence rate accounts for how well accepted proposals combine.
infographic.evidence_signal: In GPT-OSS-120B robot-routing tests, three agents found collision-free plans in every run; on a larger task, six agents searched about twice as fast as a single agent in median, and merging the best checked combination cut team search time by about 30%.
infographic.watch_item: Practical gains depend on the cost of global checks and the accuracy of cross-agent corrections; approximate corrections can leave a nonzero error floor.
infographic.paper_title: Local Work, Global Progress: A Convergence Theory of AI Agent Collaboration

title: SympFormer: Inertial Attention Blocks from Damped Hamiltonian Dynamics on Spaces of Probability Measures
authors: Viktor Stein, Levin Maier, Wuchen Li, Gabriele Steidl
abstract: The attention mechanism underpins modern large language models, yet their dynamics remain only partially understood. Recent perspectives interpret attention blocks as interacting particle systems, whose mean-field limits correspond to gradient flows of energy functionals on spaces of probability densities on $\mathbb R^d$ equipped with Wasserstein-type metrics. We extend this viewpoint by deriving accelerated attention blocks from inertial, Nesterov-type damped Hamiltonian dynamics on these density spaces, developing the geometry and differential calculus needed to make the construction rigorous. In particular, we introduce a local-mobility geometry for the Otto-Wasserstein and softmax-Wasserstein settings, and a quotient Stein geometry that resolves the degeneracy of the linear-attention kernel to yield a well-defined metric and differential calculus. We provide rigorous foundations when softmax attention admits a gradient-flow formulation and when its inertial counterpart admits a damped Hamiltonian on explicitly characterized domains. For linear attention, we obtain a finite-dimensional solution theory with sharp conditions for global existence versus finite-time second-moment blow-up. We further prove a quantitative link between continuous moment blow-up and the discrete-layer depth at which token norms cross a prescribed threshold. Finally, motivated by the finite-token geometry, we propose geometric corrections to token and momentum updates. In decoder-only, nanoGPT-style experiments on TinyStories and OpenWebText, these corrections lower validation negative log-likelihood on next-token prediction relative to momentum-only controls.

infographic.key_insight: SympFormer derives accelerated attention blocks from inertial, damped Hamiltonian dynamics on spaces of probability measures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This geometric framework motivates token and momentum corrections that improve next-token prediction over momentum-only controls in nanoGPT-style experiments.
method: Develop local-mobility geometry for Otto- and softmax-Wasserstein settings and quotient Stein geometry for linear attention.
Establish conditions for gradient-flow and damped Hamiltonian formulations, plus global existence versus moment blow-up for linear attention.
Translate finite-token geometry into corrected token and momentum updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Decoder-only experiments on TinyStories and OpenWebText report lower validation negative log-likelihood with geometric corrections than with momentum-only controls.
infographic.watch_item: The theory requires characterized domains and conditions; reported experiments do not establish stability or performance at large-model scale.
infographic.paper_title: SympFormer: Inertial Attention Blocks from Damped Hamiltonian Dynamics on Spaces of Probability Measures
